passage: Three days before the school assembly in their Pune colony school, Usha's speech on water shortage was a wall of facts. She read it to her friend Nikita on the terrace, and Nikita's eyes drifted to the kites. "You lost me at the second number," Nikita admitted. Usha was stung, but she tried again. This time she started with a question: "Who here had a bucket bath this morning because the tank was empty?" Then three points, one story about her building's tanker, and a closing line. On the day, her knees shook and her mouth went dry. She held the mic stand, found Nikita's face in the third row, and asked her question. Half the hall raised their hands. Someone laughed. Usha relaxed a little and kept going.

qa.q: What question did Usha open her speech with?
qa.a: She asked who had a bucket bath that morning because the tank was empty.

qa.q: How did Usha feel when Nikita said, "You lost me at the second number"?
qa.a: She felt stung and a bit hurt, but she took it as a sign the speech was not working and chose to fix it.

qa.q: What helped Usha keep going when her knees shook?
qa.a: Holding the mic stand, finding a friendly face and starting with a question that got hands up gave her something steady and made the audience part of the talk.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel sitting in the third row during the speech?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt proud and a little responsible, since that honest comment helped Usha change the opening that now held the hall.

grounding: It shows a teen restructuring a talk around a question and story, managing stage fear and holding the audience's attention.

passage:
"Didi, you're talking to the wall again."
"I'm practising, Sachin. Go away."
"Why are you whispering, though? The hall is huge."
Disha lowered her notes. "Because if I say it loud and mess up, it's real."
"Say it to me. I'm eleven. I don't count."
She sighed and started. "Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about—" She stopped. "My voice is shaking."
"So? Mine shakes when I ask Papa for money."
She laughed despite herself. "Okay. Again."
"Slower. And look at me, not the paper."
"Since when are you a coach?"
"Since you started whispering at walls."
The third time, she got through the first minute without looking down. Sachin clapped with his feet on the sofa. "Now do it louder."

qa.q: How old does Sachin say he is?
qa.a: He says he is eleven.

qa.q: Why was Disha whispering her speech?
qa.a: She was afraid that saying it loudly and making a mistake would make her failure feel real, so whispering felt safer.

qa.q: Which of Sachin's tips helped, and why?
qa.a: Telling her to go slower and look at him instead of the paper gave her a real listener, so she got through the first minute without looking down.

qa.q: What is it like for Sachin to coach his older sister?
qa.a: He seems to enjoy it and feel useful, teasing her while also cheering her on by clapping. 🙂

grounding: It shows a teen practising a speech at home, facing stage fear with a sibling's help and building delivery.

passage: Last year I was picked to speak at the district science fair, and I nearly said no. I'm Imran, and until then I had never spoken to more than my own class. My plan was to memorise everything. On the day, the first sentence came out and then my mind went blank. I stood there, hearing the fan. Sangeeta Ma'am, our physics teacher, was holding up my cue card from the front row. I read one word, "magnets," and the rest came back. Later she told me people remember stories more than scripts. So this year I built the talk on three cards: the problem, what we tried, the moment it failed. My hands were still cold. But I looked up more, and people actually laughed at the failure part.

qa.q: What was the one word Imran read from the cue card?
qa.a: Imran read the word "magnets."

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when Imran's mind went blank?
qa.a: Imran was frozen with fear, standing silent and hearing only the fan, as if the memorised script had vanished.

qa.q: What changed in how Imran prepared this year, and why did it help?
qa.a: Imran built the talk on three cards around a story instead of memorising a script, so one cue could bring back the whole flow.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Ma'am have felt holding up the card in the front row?
qa.a: She was probably anxious for Imran but ready to help, and then glad when one word got him going again.

grounding: A teen looks back on freezing during a talk and learning to structure speeches around cues and a story.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 10 assembly, Monday. Tejas (15) gave his first assembly talk today, on why our school should start a seed library. Last week in rehearsal he spoke to the floor and rushed through in two minutes. We worked on a shape: open with a short story, three points, close with one request. Today his knees were visibly shaking at the mic. He opened with the story of his grandmother's tomato seeds, and a few juniors laughed at the right moment. Halfway through he lost his place. He stopped, breathed, glanced at his card, looked at the front row and carried on. He ended by asking, 'Who'll bring one packet of seeds?' Hands went up. Next step: I've asked him to coach the Class 8 speakers. — Hrithik Sir

qa.q: What was Tejas's talk about?
qa.a: Why the school should start a seed library.

qa.q: How can you tell Tejas was afraid at the mic?
qa.a: His knees were visibly shaking, and in rehearsal he had spoken to the floor and rushed.

qa.q: What helped Tejas recover when he lost his place?
qa.a: He paused, breathed, checked his card and looked at the front row before continuing, instead of panicking.

qa.q: How might the juniors in the audience have experienced the talk?
qa.a: They were drawn in by the grandmother's seed story and felt invited to act when Tejas asked for seeds.

grounding: A teacher records a teen structuring a talk, handling stage fear and holding an audience.

passage: Thursday, 10 pm. Youth parliament done!!! Writing this before I forget how it felt. Woke up at five with my stomach in knots. Hansa made me practise twice on the terrace, once to her and once to the water tank, and made me slow down. She said, 'Say your first line like you're telling me a secret.' At the district hall there were about two hundred people. My voice cracked on 'Honourable Speaker' and someone giggled. I wanted to vanish. But I did the thing: feet flat, one breath, looked at the kind uncle in the second row. Then I told the story of our village's broken handpump, and the hall went quiet. Quiet in a good way. I actually held them. Me! Santosh!

qa.q: Where did Santosh practise before the youth parliament?
qa.a: On the terrace, once to Hansa and once to the water tank.

qa.q: What did Santosh feel when his voice cracked and someone giggled?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and wanted to vanish, but then steadied himself.

qa.q: Which of Santosh's techniques could help another nervous speaker?
qa.a: Planting feet flat, taking one breath, finding a kind face and opening with a real story.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel reading this diary entry?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and happy that her practice sessions helped him hold the hall. 😊

grounding: A teen records managing stage fear and holding an audience with a practised talk.

passage:
At the gram sabha meeting in their village near Madurai, the panchayat hall was full of older men. Lakshmi, sixteen, stood up with a sheet of paper in her shaking hand.
Her brother Hrithik had helped her practise all week under the neem tree. “Say what's wrong, why it matters, what you want,” he'd said.
She began. “The girls' toilet at our school has been broken for four months.” A few men muttered. She looked at the back wall, as she'd practised, and kept going. “Twelve girls stopped coming to school. I'm asking the panchayat to fix it before the exams.”
The hall went quiet. The sarpanch nodded slowly and asked for a quote from the mason.
Outside, Hrithik slapped her on the back. Her legs were still trembling.

qa.q: How long had the girls' toilet been broken?
qa.a: It had been broken for four months.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel as she stood up to speak?
qa.a: She felt nervous and scared, her hand shaking and her legs trembling.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi hold the audience's attention?
qa.a: A clear structure of problem, reason and request, and looking at the back wall to stay steady.

qa.q: How might the sarpanch have seen Lakshmi's speech?
qa.a: He probably saw it as clear and serious, which is why he asked for a quote from the mason.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old structures a talk and manages fear to speak at a village meeting.

passage:
In a school hall in Kyoto, Hana, fourteen, waited behind the curtain for the speech contest. Her palms were wet. Her talk was about her grandfather's bicycle repair shop.
Her friend Aiko squeezed her arm. “Remember: pick three friendly faces. Left, middle, right. Talk to them, not the crowd.”
Hana walked out. For the first line, her voice wobbled. She found Aiko in the middle, then a kind-looking teacher on the left, then a boy smiling on the right. She talked to them.
She told the story of the old bicycle her grandfather rebuilt for her. People laughed at the part where the bell fell off.
When she finished, the applause was loud. She didn't win, but three people came up to ask about the shop.

qa.q: What was Hana's talk about?
qa.a: Her grandfather's bicycle repair shop.

qa.q: How did Hana feel waiting behind the curtain?
qa.a: She felt nervous, with wet palms.

qa.q: What technique helped Hana hold the audience?
qa.a: Talking to three friendly faces instead of the whole crowd, and telling a story.

qa.q: How might Aiko feel watching Hana's speech?
qa.a: Aiko probably feels proud and happy that the tip helped.

grounding: A fourteen-year-old manages stage fear and holds an audience with a story.

passage:
The school hall was packed for Monday assembly, and Ritu's hands were damp around her three index cards. Her topic: why the school should start a recycling drive.
Backstage, Afreen squeezed her arm. "Remember the plan. Story, three points, one ask."
Ritu walked to the mic. Four hundred faces. Her mind went blank for a second. She looked at the first card: "The bin behind the canteen."
"Last week," she began, "I counted forty plastic bottles in one bin behind our canteen."
A few students looked up. Her voice steadied. She made her three points, pausing after each, and ended: "Bring one bottle to the green box on Friday."
Afreen was clapping hardest. On Friday, the green box was overflowing.

qa.q: How many plastic bottles did Ritu count in one bin?
qa.a: Forty plastic bottles.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when her mind went blank?
qa.a: Ritu felt a jolt of stage fright facing so many people.

qa.q: Which part of Ritu's plan helped her hold the audience?
qa.a: Starting with a real story, keeping to three points, and ending with one clear request kept the talk focused and memorable.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel when the green box overflows on Friday?
qa.a: Afreen probably feels proud of Ritu and happy that the speech actually worked 🎉.

grounding: A teen structures an assembly talk and manages stage fear to move her audience.

passage:
Dear Lalremsiami didi,
You asked how my first district-level speech went. Honestly? My knees were shaking so hard I thought the audience could see.
I used your trick. I didn't memorise every word. Just the opening line, three key points on a card, and the closing line. When I forgot what came next, I looked at the card, took a breath, and carried on.
The best part was the story about my grandfather's village well. The hall went quiet. I could feel them listening.
I came third. My friends said I sounded calm. I didn't feel calm! But now I know that fear doesn't show as much as I thought.
Thank you for making me practise in front of the mirror.
Chinmay

qa.q: Where did Chinmay put the three key points?
qa.a: On a card.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling with knees shaking so hard?
qa.a: Chinmay felt very nervous and afraid the audience could see the fear.

qa.q: Which of Lalremsiami's tips worked best for Chinmay, and why?
qa.a: Memorising only the opening, closing and key points on a card let Chinmay recover when the words ran out, instead of panicking.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Lalremsiami would likely feel proud and happy that her advice helped Chinmay get through a first big speech.

grounding: A teen writes to a mentor about managing stage fear and structuring a speech.

passage:
Uday, you asked about my first big speech, so here it is. I'm Tarun, and I used to be the kid who'd pretend to be sick on presentation days.
Class 11, I had to give a talk at the science fair opening. Two hundred people. I wrote the whole thing out, word for word, and on the morning I couldn't remember line one.
My teacher said, "Forget the script. What's the one thing you want them to remember?" I said, "That the river near our school is dying." She said, "Start there."
So I did. I started with a photo of the river. I told them what I'd seen, then what we could do. I didn't read anything.
My voice shook for the first minute. Then people started nodding, and I forgot to be scared. That's when I learnt: people don't need you perfect. They need you clear.

qa.q: How many people were at the science fair opening?
qa.a: Two hundred people.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling on the morning he couldn't remember line one?
qa.a: Tarun felt panicked and anxious, with the fully written script failing him.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned Tarun's speech around?
qa.a: Dropping the script and starting from the one thing Tarun wanted people to remember, the dying river, with a photo.

qa.q: How might Tarun's teacher have seen the speech?
qa.a: The teacher probably felt proud, seeing Tarun connect with the audience once the talk came from what Tarun cared about.

grounding: A young person tells a podcast host how Tarun learned to structure a talk around one clear message.

passage:
I'm Ritu. I sat in the third row of assembly the day Rajni gave the talk on our school's water problem.
When she walked up, her index cards were shaking so much I could hear them. For the first few seconds she looked only at the floor. Then she did something odd: she stopped, took a breath, and looked straight at the back wall, above everyone's heads.
She started with a question: "How many of you found the second-floor tap dry today?" Hands went up. People laughed. After that she had us.
She had three points, one per card, and she ended with a small ask: report leaks on the chart outside the staffroom.
Her voice still wobbled on the last line. I can't say if she was still scared. But she didn't rush.

qa.q: How did Rajni start her talk?
qa.a: She started with a question: "How many of you found the second-floor tap dry today?"

qa.q: What do Rajni's shaking cards suggest about how she felt at first?
qa.a: They suggest Rajni was very nervous and afraid of the audience when she walked up.

qa.q: Which of Rajni's choices helped her hold the audience, and why?
qa.a: Opening with a question about something everyone had experienced made people laugh and pay attention, and three simple points kept it clear.

qa.q: How might the students in the hall have seen Rajni's talk?
qa.a: They probably felt included and interested, because the question was about their own day, so they listened rather than judged her nerves.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a teen managing stage fear and holding an audience with a clear structure.

passage:
Monday. Hafsa practised her science fair talk on her friend Maria in the library corner. It went everywhere: solar ovens, her cousin in Rajasthan, a video she'd seen. After four minutes, Maria asked, "Wait, what's the point?" Hafsa groaned and put her head on the desk.
Wednesday. Maria helped her cut it down to three parts: the problem, how her oven works, what she measured. One sentence each on a card. Hafsa practised in front of the mirror, then in front of her little brother, who kept yawning on purpose.
Friday, the fair. Halfway through, a judge asked a question and Hafsa's mind went blank. She glanced at card two, took a breath and said, "Let me come back to that." She finished, then answered it properly.
Maria gave her a thumbs up from behind the judges.

qa.q: What three parts did Maria help Hafsa cut the talk into?
qa.a: The problem, how her oven works, and what she measured.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling on Monday when she put her head on the desk?
qa.a: Hafsa felt frustrated and discouraged, because her talk had rambled and Maria couldn't find the point.

qa.q: What could someone with a blank mind on stage learn from Hafsa's Friday?
qa.a: Keep a simple card for each part, glance at it, breathe, and say you'll come back to a question rather than panicking.

qa.q: How might Maria feel watching Hafsa recover in front of the judges?
qa.a: Maria probably feels proud and relieved, since Maria helped build the structure that saved the moment.

grounding: Illustrates, over several days, a teen structuring a talk and handling a moment of stage fear.

passage:
Pradeep, before you go up to speak at that conference, let me tell you about my first speech.
I was fifteen. Our school's annual day. I had learned four pages by heart. I walked up, saw six hundred faces and my mind went white. I stood there. Somebody coughed. I could hear the fans.
Then Mr Joseph, our English teacher, walked to the side of the stage and held up a card he'd made me write: "Why I love trains." Just that. I'd told him the whole speech was about my grandfather's railway job.
So I dropped the pages and told them about the night mail and my grandfather's lantern. Five minutes. People clapped properly.
Since then I never learn speeches by heart. I learn the story. That's what your Rafiq Chacha knows.

qa.q: What did Mr Joseph hold up at the side of the stage?
qa.a: He held up a card that said "Why I love trains."

qa.q: How did young Rafiq feel when his mind went white?
qa.a: Young Rafiq felt frozen with fear, standing silent in front of six hundred faces.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Dropping the memorised pages to tell the real story of his grandfather worked, because he was speaking from memory and feeling instead of recitation.

qa.q: How might Mr Joseph have felt standing at the side of the stage?
qa.a: Mr Joseph was probably anxious for his student and then relieved and proud when the card helped him recover.

grounding: Shows an elder recounting how, as a teen, he overcame stage fear by telling a story rather than reciting.

passage:
Hansa had practised her Annual Day speech on water conservation for two weeks: a story to open, three points, a question to close. She was on third. Then, as she reached the podium, the microphone died with a squeal. Four hundred students and parents stirred and started chatting.
Her hands went cold. Her friend Jomon, running the sound desk, mouthed, "Two minutes!"
Hansa didn't wait. She stepped to the front edge of the stage, planted her feet like her drama teacher taught, and said loudly, "Raise your hand if your tap ran dry this summer."
Hands shot up. The chatter stopped.
She spoke slower than in practice, looking at the back row, pausing after each point. When the mic crackled back on halfway through, she waved it away.
Afterwards, Jomon handed her a bottle of water. "You didn't even need me."

qa.q: How many students and parents were in the audience?
qa.a: Four hundred students and parents.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when the microphone died?
qa.a: Hansa felt nervous, her hands going cold, but she chose to act instead of freezing.

qa.q: What choice kept the audience with Hansa, and why?
qa.a: Asking a question that everyone could answer with a raised hand, because it pulled attention back to her without needing the microphone.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel watching from the sound desk?
qa.a: Jomon probably felt stressed about the broken mic at first, then relieved and proud when Hansa held the audience on her own.

grounding: Shows a teenager using a clear structure and calm stage habits to hold an audience when the microphone fails.
